trace: The ask on NVDA is a probability-weighted 6-9 month forecast, so before I write anything I need to decide where the real uncertainty sits. My visibility into Data Center demand is genuinely good, so I'll put fundamental driver confidence at 85 percent, but competitive dynamics are murkier at 70 percent and the macro rate path is the weakest link at 60 percent, with valuation sensitivity around 75 percent. That spread should drive the scenario weights. The central story is that dominance persists but growth normalizes, Data Center decelerating from triple digits to something like 80-90 percent YoY, Blackwell landing on schedule, gross margin holding near 75-76 percent, and quarterly free cash flow above 20 billion. On that I get a 42x forward multiple on roughly 3.45 of annualized forward EPS, which is 145, and I'll call that 60 percent likely with 70 percent confidence. The bull path needs a genuine demand pull-forward plus competitor stumbles, a decisive break above 140 on volume 150 percent of the 50-day average with ADX over 40, and gets me to 180 at 25 percent. Bear at 95 with 15 percent weight. Now the honest problem: I've lived through the run and I'm probably anchoring on continued outperformance, so 15 percent on the bear may be too generous to the bulls when price-to-sales sits near 30x versus a tech-sector historical 8-10x. The consolidation between 110 and 130 could be distribution, not a healthy pause. Weighting it out gives 146.25, only marginally above spot, which forces the conclusion honestly: hold and accumulate on weakness rather than chase, buy near the 50-day EMA, stop on a weekly close under the 100-day around 105, cap size at 5-7 percent. And I should name what would prove me wrong first: CoWoS packaging guidance from TSM, hyperscaler capex language about optimization, and any sequential gross margin slip below 74 percent.

Adobe at 560 is the kind of name where the fundamentals are easy and the judgment is hard. The moat is real, cash flow is real, so I'd put fundamental strength confidence around 85 percent. But the whole question over the next 6-12 months is Figma, and my honest confidence in the synergy case is only 50 percent, with valuation confidence maybe 60 percent given how rate-sensitive a 29x multiple is. Blend those and the overall thesis sits at about 65 percent, medium-high, not conviction. Base case: integration proceeds, Firefly retains users but only moves Creative Cloud ARPU 2-3 percent, and 29x forward, in line with the five-year average, gets me 625 at 60 percent probability. Bull needs both rapid cross-sell above 15 percent and Firefly lifting ARPU more than 5 percent alongside a soft landing, so 35x and 750, but I'll only give that 25 percent. Bear is the regulatory block, UK and EU killing the deal with a billion-dollar termination fee plus a recession compressing enterprise budgets more than 10 percent, 22x and 450, at 15 percent. The bias I need to flag against myself is confirmation bias toward the incumbent, because AI-native competitors like Midjourney are exactly the sort of leaner threat an established-leader framing underrates. Stress-testing zero synergy plus a five percent enterprise spending decline still lands around 510, so downside from here is maybe ten percent buffered. That combination, modest base upside to 625 with a real fat tail either way, argues for hold rather than a full buy. I'd scale in toward the 200-day near 490, add on regulatory approval, trim into 625, and exit on a weekly close below 490. Early warnings: Figma power-user churn chatter, gross margin under 87 percent, and Dylan Field or other key Figma leaders leaving within twelve months. Most likely failure is synergy disappointment at 35 percent, drifting to 500.

Palantir over six months is a valuation-sentiment problem more than an execution problem, and I want my confidence scores to say that plainly. Chart structure is fairly readable so I'll call technicals 75 percent, but the fundamentals deserve only 60 percent because the true TAM and the durability of GAAP profitability are genuinely contested, and my scenario probabilities themselves I'd only stand behind at 65 percent given how news-driven this high-beta name is. The base case is continuation, not inflection: total revenue up 18-22 percent YoY, US commercial compounding around 35-40 percent, a third and fourth straight GAAP-profitable quarter putting S&P 500 inclusion in play, net margin 3-5 percent. Technically that means holding above the 200-day near 21.50 with RSI parked between 50 and 65 and volume-profile support at 22-24. Applying roughly 19x forward sales, slightly below where it trades now, gives me 29, and I'll weight that 60 percent. Bull is an AIP adoption inflection with a marquee government or enterprise deal, 25 percent. Bear is multiple compression toward the 12-14x industry median, a failed retest of the 200-day, RSI under 30, and 19 as the target. The self-critique writes itself: I am almost certainly carrying recency bias from the AIP narrative and the profitability headlines, and there's narrative fallacy risk in making a tidy story out of a lumpy business. The honest alternative is that this consolidation is institutional distribution rather than accumulation, and I'd put 20 percent on that. My single biggest vulnerability is that the whole multiple rests on commercial growth, since government revenue is stable but lumpy and doesn't earn a premium. So the early-warning list is net dollar retention slipping below 115 percent, stock-based comp climbing back over 30 percent of revenue, and heavy insider selling from Karp and the executive bench.

The framing here is government versus commercial for Palantir over twelve months, and that split is exactly where the valuation question lives. Government is the visible, stable leg growing maybe 15-18 percent YoY; commercial is the speculative leg that has to carry the multiple. So my fundamental confidence is 70 percent, technicals only 60 percent given volatility and news sensitivity, scenario modeling 65 percent, and I'll headline overall confidence at 65 percent, cautiously optimistic rather than bullish. Base case has commercial accelerating to 40-45 percent YoY with US commercial customer count up 40 percent, operating margins holding 20-22 percent, and four consecutive GAAP-profitable quarters clearing the S&P 500 hurdle. I apply 18x forward sales, a deliberate discount to growth peers because of government contract concentration, cross-checked against a DCF at 10 percent WACC and 4 percent terminal growth, which gives 27 at 60 percent probability. Bull needs commercial above 60 percent for two straight quarters plus a hyperscaler or major consulting partnership, and I'd stretch to 25x sales for 42 at 25 percent, with sensitivity showing each 5 percent of extra commercial growth worth about 3 dollars. Bear is de-rating to 12x forward sales as the growth story stalls. Weighting those out lands at 28.55, which is my headline target. Against myself: I am leaning on narrative bias about AIP without long-run evidence, and the base case probably underweights stock-based compensation as a drag. Insider selling I've read as routine diversification, but the bearish read that it signals doubt deserves 30 percent. Early warnings are US commercial decelerating toward the low 30s, adjusted operating margin under 20 percent, and rising top-20 customer concentration. Most likely failure is a sales cycle that won't shorten, 25 percent odds, roughly 30 percent downside.

Lululemon comes down to two forces pulling opposite ways: a normalizing North American consumer against international expansion that still has runway. I'll build the base case on that offset, with revenue compounding 12-14 percent, operating margin steady at 21-22 percent as supply chain efficiency pays for higher marketing, and international climbing from about 18 percent of revenue to 25 percent by FY2025. At 28x forward, its own five-year average, that's 410 over 12-18 months, and I'll assign 55 percent since neither leg is a stretch. Technically the setup supports patience rather than conviction, consolidating above the 200-day with RSI near 50 and a neutral MACD, so the chart is waiting on a catalyst rather than confirming one. Bull at 25 percent requires a soft landing plus a China rebound above 35 percent YoY and footwear taking 2 percent of the premium athletic market a year early, with 150bps of gross margin expansion, and I'd pay 35x for that, giving 525. I'd also note the transmission channel: 50bps off the ten-year lifts discretionary multiples roughly 10 percent, which is a big part of the bull math. Bear at 20 percent is trade-down plus Alo and Vuori taking share, 300bps of gross margin compression and inventory days up 20 percent forcing write-downs. Honestly, my fundamental confidence is only 65 percent because a P/E near 30 leaves no margin of safety, versus 75 percent on technicals where the long-term uptrend is intact. I should admit confirmation bias toward the brand and possible underestimation of niche DTC competitors, and give 30 percent to the reading that North American softness is saturation rather than normalization. Warning signs: two quarters of gross margin below 55 percent, inventory outgrowing sales by more than 10 percent, and a sustained break of the 200-day at 365. The likeliest failure at 40 percent is pure multiple compression on solid execution.

Three moving parts here for NVDA and they don't move together: AI data center demand, a gaming cycle that is only now recovering, and semiconductor geopolitics. I'd set overall confidence at 70 percent because I have real conviction on the demand driver but the valuation and macro overlay cut against it. In the base case, which I'll weight 60 percent, data center grows 90 percent YoY and decelerates toward 45 percent over twelve months, gaming returns to 15 percent growth, ROE stays north of 60 percent, and export controls end up targeted rather than catastrophic. A 38x multiple on FY2026 consensus gets me 145 over six to nine months, which against a forward P/E near 40x and a projected 35 percent five-year EPS CAGR is defensible. The chart mostly supports that: holding above the 50-day EMA, RSI over 50, a high-volume node right around current price, though the MACD is threatening a bearish crossover even with the histogram still positive, so I should flag that rather than ignore it. Bull at 25 percent needs a steeper adoption curve plus a US-China thaw and automotive and Omniverse crossing 10 percent of revenue, and I'd pay 45x for 180, with sensitivity of roughly 8 dollars per 5 percent data center beat. Bear at 15 percent is an AI air pocket plus AMD and Gaudi share gains and hard export controls, compressing to 28x for 95, with a head-and-shoulders top and falling OBV. That leaves accumulate-on-weakness rather than chase: phase in at 120-125 near the 50-day, add above 140, cut on a weekly close under the 200-day around 90. My bias risk is recency, and the honest counter is that 60 percent on the base may be too conservative if this is early innings. Watch gross margin under 70 percent, inventory days spiking, and R&D moving sharply either way.

Block is really two businesses with opposite macro sensitivities, and the nine-month call hinges on whether Cash App growth can carry a cyclically exposed Square seller book. That asymmetry is why my macro confidence is only 50 percent even though I'd put fundamentals at 75 percent and technicals at 60 percent, landing overall thesis confidence at 65 percent. Base case, 60 percent weight, is a soft landing with GDP around 1.5-2.0 percent: Cash App gross profit up 18-22 percent on rising monthly transacting actives and better monetization through Card and Borrow, while Square seller gross profit slows to 8-10 percent as SMBs meet tighter credit, with international softening the blow. Adjusted EBITDA margin expands 100-150bps on cost discipline. At roughly 4.5x forward EV to gross profit that's 85. The chart agrees it's a base, not a trend: oscillating between the 200-week around 50 and resistance near 90, daily RSI stuck between 40 and 60. Bull at 25 percent needs a high-margin Cash App product lifting ARPU plus GDP above 2.5 percent and a dovish pivot re-accelerating Square GPV past 15 percent, giving 6.0x and 120. With the stock around 65 to 70, the base case alone offers enough upside to start buying, so I'd scale: a third now, a third on a 50-day EMA retest, the last third on a weekly close above 95 on 1.5x volume, and cut half on a weekly close below 58. Where I might be wrong: I may be underweighting Apple's financial services ambitions, so 15 percent on the bear could be light, and this consolidation could be a bearish pennant rather than a base. Failure indicators are Square GPV growth under 5 percent, net new MTAs under a million for two quarters, and margins that refuse to expand.

For this NVDA read the emphasis is competitive landscape plus macro over six to nine months, and I want the base case to sit on order backlog rather than enthusiasm. If Blackwell and H100/H200 demand stays robust while growth normalizes, data center at 90 percent YoY down from over 200, gaming back to 15 percent, net margins holding near 55 percent and share above 80 percent even as MI300X and hyperscaler silicon get some traction, then 40x forward is fair and gives 145. That's 60 percent probability, with a volume profile building support at 110-120 and RSI in the 50-70 band, controlled strength rather than froth. The macro assumption embedded there matters: inflation easing to 2.5-3.0 percent and one or two 25bps cuts. Bull at 25 percent is ecosystem lock-in through software and InfiniBand plus competitor stumbles, 50x for 180, and each 5 percent of surprise data center growth is worth about 8 dollars of fair value. Bear at 15 percent runs the transmission chain explicitly: a hawkish Fed lifting borrowing costs 150bps, enterprise AI budgets cut 20 percent, a 10-12 percent data center revenue miss. Overall I'll say 75 percent thesis confidence because the backlog is concrete and the uncertainty is macro timing, not demand existence. The critique I owe myself is that I'm probably underrating how fast competitors ramp and how motivated customers are to dual-source, and there's recency bias in extrapolating hyper-growth. The genuinely scary alternative, maybe 10 percent, is that this is a one-time build-out rather than a secular cycle, and demand falls off once hyperscalers finish. So: initiate now, add on 50-day EMA pullbacks, reduce on a weekly close below the 100-day, and watch ODM channel inventory at Supermicro, two straight quarters of data center ASP decline, and lead times shortening abruptly.

Eli Lilly over twelve months is a bet on whether a massively expanding obesity TAM can absorb competition without price erosion. My fundamental thesis confidence is high at 85 percent because Mounjaro and Zepbound uptake is visible, but scenario probability confidence drops to 70 percent and price target confidence to 65 percent given how wide the outcome range is. Base case at 60 percent: revenue up 25-30 percent YoY on the GLP-1 franchise, operating margins expanding 150bps on scale, ROIC above 30 percent, donanemab approved with a slow ramp, and Novo absorbed without a price war. At 55x forward on FY2025 EPS, consistent with the premium it already carries, that's 950. Technically the trend supports it, holding the 50-week EMA with long-term ADX above 40, which is a genuinely powerful trend signature. Bull at 25 percent needs Zepbound beating the high end of guidance by more than 20 percent, competitor manufacturing setbacks, and strong orforglipron data, and I'd model it as a DCF with a 35 percent three-year revenue CAGR and 4 percent terminal growth, implying roughly 70x and 1,200. Bear at 15 percent is real price competition plus a pipeline failure, compressing to 38x for 680, which happens to line up with the 200-week average, a level untouched in years. The uncomfortable part is that everything rests on one narrative, TTM P/E is above 100x, and I should say plainly that 60 percent on the base may be complacent. That still argues for accumulate on weakness rather than chase: add on 50-day EMA dips, trim 10-15 percent above 1,200, reduce hard on a confirmed price war or a safety flag or a 200-day break. If LLY underperforms XPH by more than 10 percent in a month, I check IQVIA weekly scripts, PBM formulary news, and competitor trial and pricing headlines.

CrowdStrike's whole argument reduces to one tension: best-in-class growth and platform consolidation against a multiple that assumes it never stops. Base case, and I'd give it 60 percent with 75 percent confidence, is flawless continued execution at 30-35 percent revenue growth, ARR growth above 30 percent, dollar-based net retention over 120 percent, and ROE improving from 15 percent toward 20 percent as profitability scales, with Falcon extending into cloud workload protection and identity. Applying 15x forward EV to sales, a modest compression from where it trades, gives a twelve-month target of 410. Technicals back that up rather than lead it, above the 200-day, weekly MACD positive, RSI between 50 and 70. Bull at 25 percent requires competitor missteps and an AI-winner narrative, maybe a SIEM or data observability acquisition, revenue pushing toward 40 percent, and the mechanism is explicit: roughly three turns of EV/sales per 5 percent of sustained growth. Bear compresses to 10x forward sales in line with the broader software group, 275, which is the number that keeps position sizing moderate. The weakness I have to name is Microsoft Defender's distribution advantage, which no amount of product superiority fully answers, and the fact that a high price-to-sales assumes a rational market that may not persist. The fair counterpoint is a scarcity premium for the only pure-play best-of-breed leader, which could keep it expensive for years and make 275 too harsh. So I'll recommend tiered entry rather than a full position: a third near the 50-day EMA, a third after a Q2 print confirming ARR above 30 percent, exit on a weekly close under the 200-day. My early warnings are the share of customers running five or more modules turning down, sales and marketing rising as a percent of revenue, and sales-cycle commentary from SentinelOne and Palo Alto.

Working through NVDA on a 12-18 month view, the question the framework forces me to answer is whether AI demand is secular or approaching saturation, and I want the numbers to arbitrate rather than the narrative. Technically the trend is unambiguous, price above the 20, 50 and 200-day EMAs, but a daily RSI of 78 is stretched and the MACD histogram is converging, so near-term I expect consolidation with the 50-day EMA at 110 as the line that matters. Fundamentally the business is pristine: ROE of 91 percent, gross margins 75-77 percent, forward P/E around 45x against roughly 85 percent projected EPS growth. My base case at 60 percent assumes FY2025 revenue of 115 billion and EPS of 2.80, data center decelerating to 80 percent YoY with share above 80 percent, which at 46.4x gives 130. Bull at 25 percent needs Blackwell revenue 30 percent above forecast plus AI software and inference passing 15 percent of revenue, taking me to 175. Bear at 15 percent is a Taiwan supply shock or AMD and Intel taking more than 15 points of share, and that's 90. Probability-weighting lands at 132, essentially where the stock trades, and that is the whole answer: the price already embeds the base case, so this is a hold, not a buy, with an ideal entry only on a pullback into 110-115 and a hard stop at 95. Stress-testing, valuation still holds above 100 with growth decelerating to 50 percent, but the thesis genuinely breaks if gross margin sits under 72 percent for two quarters. I should own the anchoring bias to recent results and admit I can't distinguish true end-demand from customer inventory build. So I'll watch inventory days at MSFT, GOOGL and META, competitor win announcements, and any cut to TSMC's CoWoS expansion plans.

Micron at 130.50 is a cycle call more than a company call, and I should be explicit that my confidence is uneven: 85 percent that the memory upturn is real, 75 percent on the technical setup, but only 50 percent on valuation because forward estimates in this industry are notoriously unreliable. Base case at 60 percent is that DRAM and NAND pricing keeps rising sequentially on disciplined supply and HBM demand, PCs and smartphones recover modestly, and MU ramps HBM3E into meaningful share. Revenue up 55-65 percent YoY for two quarters, ROE swinging from negative to plus 15 percent by early 2025, and at 5.5x forward price-to-sales, a mid-cycle multiple, that's 155. The chart supports it, holding the 50-day EMA at 121 with weekly MACD bullish and OBV confirming accumulation, though RSI oscillating between 60 and 80 means I'm buying strength, not value. Bull at 25 percent needs HBM pricing power beyond expectations and possibly competitor supply disruption, gross margins past the 35 percent target, 7.0x sales and 190, with ADX above 40 on a break of the psychological 150. Because the entry is overbought, the honest recommendation is a conditional buy staged in thirds: one at 130, one on a 50-day retest at 121, one above 140, taking half off at 155 and trailing the rest toward 190, with a hard stop at 118. The self-critique is that the bullish narrative is consensus right now and confirmation bias is a live risk, and I'd assign 20 percent to reading RSI over 75 far above the 200-day as a blow-off top instead of strength. If 118 breaks I check DRAMeXchange spot prices, Samsung and Hynix guidance, and MU's inventory days. Most likely failure is a false peak, telegraphed by flattening OBV and bearish MACD divergence.

The Lilly question I keep circling is not whether GLP-1 demand exists, it plainly does, but whether the price already assumes flawless execution. That is why I'd score fundamental growth trajectory at 90 percent but valuation support at only 40 percent, with scenario probabilities at 65 percent, blending to an overall 65 percent. Base case, 60 percent probability: manufacturing scales, revenue compounds 25-30 percent YoY for two years, operating margins push past 40 percent, ROE stays above 50 percent, dual-agonist share holds above 45 percent, and IRA price negotiation doesn't bite until late in the decade. At 45x forward on 2026 EPS near 23.30 that gives 1,050 over 12-18 months. Technically I want ADX above 30, support at the 50-day EMA, and OBV still rising to confirm institutional accumulation rather than churn. Bull at 25 percent adds donanemab uptake and an orforglipron launch expanding the patient pool, 50x on 26 of EPS for 1,300, needing Zepbound beats above 15 percent per quarter. Against all that, the monthly RSI at 88 is a historical extreme, and I have to take seriously the alternative that this is speculative overextension rather than fundamental strength, because pharma mean reversions are violent. Payers forcing switches to cheaper alternatives is the risk I'm most likely underweighting. Balancing conviction against valuation, the right posture is cautious accumulation on pullbacks rather than buying here, exiting or hedging on a decisive weekly close below the 200-day around 750. Early warnings: OBV flattening while price rises, LLY script growth trailing Novo's for two straight quarters, and rising sarcopenia discussion in the literature. If it fails I check Amgen's AMG-133 and Viking's VK2735 data, CVS and Express Scripts formulary changes, and insider selling.

This NVDA request wants DCF sensitivity behind the targets, so I'll anchor each case to a discount-rate and growth pair rather than just slapping on multiples. Confidence-wise I'd say technicals 75 percent given a strong but overbought tape, fundamentals 85 percent since the growth is exceptional but rests on forward projections, and scenario modeling only 65 percent because the AI market's shape is genuinely unknown. Base case at 60 percent: share holds near 80 percent, growth decelerates from hyper-growth to 40-50 percent YoY, Blackwell transitions cleanly, forward P/E contracts toward 35x as earnings catch up, ROE stays above 60 percent, and a DCF at 30 percent five-year revenue CAGR with a 12 percent WACC supports 145 on 35x FY2026 EPS. Technically the 50-day EMA around 120 is support and OBV still confirms, though the MACD histogram is waning. Bull at 25 percent runs a 45 percent CAGR, with the transmission spelled out: 10 percent higher enterprise adoption lifts data center revenue about 15 percent and EPS about 12 percent, giving 190 at 45x. Bear at 15 percent cuts to 25x a reduced EPS for 95. Weighting gives 148.75, modestly above spot, so the call is initiate but hold capital in reserve, buy near the 50-day, add on a breakout to new highs or if data center growth re-accelerates past 60 percent, and treat a close below the 200-day near 90 as the trend break. The critique I owe: everything here hinges on DCF inputs that are hypersensitive to growth and discount rate, and 15 percent on the bear may understate semiconductor cyclicality. Fairly, an RSI above 70 can mark a power trend rather than an exhaustion signal. Watch insider selling, 13F flows, price-OBV divergence, and MSFT and META capex guidance.

Lilly over the next twelve months hinges on the Zepbound and Mounjaro trajectory against Novo, and unlike a more cautious framing I want to skew this one positive because the pipeline optionality is real. Running a Bayesian model updated on quarterly sales, I get bull at 30 percent to 1,150 on faster Zepbound uptake plus a positive donanemab decision and Novo supply trouble, base at 60 percent to 910 on linear GLP-1 growth with stable competition, and bear at only 10 percent to 720 on a safety surprise or donanemab rejection. That distribution weights out to 942 and supports a buy rather than a hold, with overall confidence around 70 percent. The base case has total GLP-1 franchise revenue above 25 billion for the year, forward P/E near 55x justified by EPS growth over 50 percent, expanding ROE and ROCE, and quarterly income beating estimates by 5-10 percent, with the FDA donanemab decision landing by Q4 2024. Technically the setup cooperates: above the 50-day EMA, MACD positive, OBV accumulating on up days. What nags at me is that a rising ATR alongside rising price can mean late-stage churn and distribution rather than healthy momentum, so I should name that alternative. Backtests on mega-cap pharma blockbuster launches show base cases hitting roughly 65 percent of the time with 20 percent drawdowns even inside intact uptrends, which argues for phased entry rather than a full position. So: half a position now between 820 and market, complete on a 50-day pullback, trim a third at 910, target 1,100, stop on a weekly close below the 100-day near 740, and size it 5-7 percent given single-franchise dependency. Earliest warning is two consecutive weeks of flattening Zepbound new scripts in IQVIA data.

If 145 fails I check Digitimes for TSMC wafer order cuts, NVDA and Intel data center commentary, and whether gross margin misses guidance.

If 235 breaks, check Chinese TOPCon and HJT module spot prices, Section 201, 301 and AD/CVD news, and whether book-to-bill drops under 1.0.

Taking AMD over six to nine months with the competitive triangle against NVIDIA and Intel front and center, I land cautiously optimistic rather than bullish. Bull at 25 percent is MI300X beating forecasts with real software ecosystem gains, 45x for 225. Bear at 15 percent is the CUDA moat proving insurmountable while Intel's new CPUs take share, 26x for 130. Probability-weighted that comes to 178.50, just above where the stock sits, which is why the tone should be constructive but not aggressive. Stress-testing zero PC market growth instead of low single digits only moves the target from 175 to about 168, so the thesis is moderately resilient to non-data-center weakness, which reassures me about the base case. The self-critique that matters most: I'm probably carrying recency bias from eighteen months of AI expansion, and I suspect the true distribution is more bimodal than my weights imply, meaning the muddle-through case deserves less than 60 percent. I also lean on management guidance, which is inherently promotional. The alternative technical read is Wyckoff distribution rather than accumulation if 155 breaks. Warning signs: data center growth decelerating sequentially while NVIDIA's accelerates, a weekly close below 150, and Digitimes reports of MI300 order cuts.

If the 200-day near 650 breaks, check customer and channel inventory.

Framing NVDA over six to twelve months, I'll blend DCF under varied growth paths with a peer multiple comparison, since neither alone is credible at this valuation. Bear is sticky inflation cooling IT budgets while MI300X plus Google TPU and Microsoft Maia take 15-20 percent share; a 15 percent cut to data center growth is about 12 percent off total revenue, compressing to 28x on a revised 26.78 EPS for 750. Because the base case upside is real but the price already discounts a lot, the honest stance is hold and accumulate on dips rather than chase: add on pullbacks to the 50-day near 900, add on a sovereign deal even at elevated levels, reduce on a weekly close below the 100-day at 780, exit on a 200-day break. With risk this asymmetric I'd also use call spreads or covered calls to shape the exposure.

Salesforce over six to twelve months boils down to one question: can it actually monetize Einstein GPT and AI Cloud fast enough to matter, while Microsoft bundles Copilot into everything. I'll put my confidence in the AI monetization thesis at only 65 percent and let that temper the whole piece. The base case at 60 percent has cRPO growing 10-12 percent YoY, AI Cloud adding about 150bps to revenue growth by the second half of 2024, non-GAAP operating margin reaching 31.5 percent and forward EPS of 9.75. Bull at 25 percent needs Fortune 100 logos taking the full AI Cloud suite, cRPO accelerating to 15-17 percent and AI Cloud adding 300-400bps, EPS 10.50 at 32x for 336, and the sensitivity I want to state is that each 1 percent of the installed base adopting the full package is roughly 500 million of FY25 revenue and about 12 dollars of fair value. Bear at 15 percent is a hard landing with two negative GDP quarters, Copilot proving good enough at a lower price, and the multiple compressing to 23x for 205; the mechanism is higher costs shrinking large enterprise pipelines about 8 percent, which hits MuleSoft and Tableau hardest. Weighting gives 278.80, comfortably above the 50-day EMA near 255, so I'll say initiate and accumulate on dips, add on a volume breakout over 280 with cRPO confirming, and use the 200-day near 230 as the tactical stop. The critique I need to voice: recent margin expansion may be layoff-driven rather than structural operating leverage, which would make the base case too generous. If 230 breaks, check billings versus revenue growth, sales attrition, and budget scrutiny language on Workday and Adobe calls.

Shortening the Palantir horizon to three to six months changes the analysis meaningfully, because in that window contract timing and multiple compression dominate fundamentals. At 20x forward EV to sales, in line with its recent average for this growth profile, I get 27, essentially the middle of the range, which is why the honest recommendation for long-term holders is hold rather than buy. Bull at 25 percent requires commercial growth above 50 percent plus a landmark contract over 100 million, expanding to 26x for 38, and I'd note each 500bps of commercial acceleration is worth roughly 2.50 of fair value. Bear at 15 percent is lengthening enterprise sales cycles plus duration risk: 100bps on the ten-year can compress high-duration multiples 10-15 percent regardless of execution, taking it to 15x and 18. So traders can work the range, with a break above 28 on volume as the bull trigger and 22 as the early bear warning, stop under the 200-day near 20.50. Self-critique: recency bias toward AIP is real and these commercial clients have not been tested over a full cycle. Fairly, heavy stock-based compensation could be talent retention rather than pure dilution. If 22 breaks, check US commercial customer count growth, government remaining deal value for pipeline decay, and executive insider sales.

Lululemon here is a very different setup from the growth-story version, because the stock is already broken technically. Going into Lululemon's earnings the technical picture is the first thing I have to respect: below the 50-day EMA near 355 and the 200-day near 390, with the 50 crossing under the 200 for a death cross, RSI around 35 oversold but unconfirmed, and multi-year pivot support at 300. Failure indicators: gross margin under 56.5 percent, international growth below 30 percent, and a third straight quarter of rising days inventory outstanding. With NVDA around 905 and Blackwell as the pivot event, the interesting question is not whether the launch succeeds but whether success is already priced. Salesforce on a twelve-month view with M&A risk in the frame is a different animal from a pure AI monetization question, and I want the capital allocation issue to carry real weight. The alternative reading I should concede is that margin gains came from layoffs rather than operational excellence, potentially damaging innovation capacity. If it breaks down, check billings versus revenue growth, cRPO growth falling under 10 percent, and Microsoft or Oracle claiming Salesforce customer wins.

Palantir on a three to six month view with contract renewals in focus, and I want my confidence to be explicitly asymmetric across segments: 85 percent on the government projection because those contracts are visible and durable, but only 60 percent on commercial given competition and macro sensitivity, blending to 70 percent overall. Albemarle is fundamentally a commodity price call dressed up as an equity analysis, so I should set overall confidence at only 65 percent and let lithium do the work. Running Monte Carlo over LCE price volatility, EV sales and project ramp schedules, the base case at 55 percent is that the lithium market floors in the second half of 2024 once battery chain destocking ends, global EV sales keep compounding 20-25 percent, and Kemerton II and Meishan come online into steady long-term agreement demand. Bull at 25 percent is a genuine price squeeze from subsidy policy or supply delays, 14.5x for 190. Bear at 20 percent, which I'll set higher than the usual because commodity troughs overstay, is prolonged weakness with LCE averaging 12,000, capex plans getting cut, and a de-rating to 8x for 95 as the story shifts from growth to distressed cyclical. From roughly 120 that's 21 percent up and 21 percent down in the two central cases, with 58 percent upside in the bull tail, which skews the risk-reward enough to justify cautious optimism: phase in at 115-125, stop below 105, take initial profits near 140. My honest vulnerability is that lithium price forecasting is close to guesswork and the EV-to-lithium demand link can decouple through inventory dynamics, plus China's processing dominance is a qualitative risk multiples don't capture. If 105 breaks, check weekly LCE spot, SQM and Ganfeng guidance revisions, and CATL and LG Chem inventories.

LVMH at 155 sits in an odd macro window, slowing global growth alongside a high-end consumer who has not blinked, and the analysis should respect both. I'll score overall confidence at 70 percent, high on fundamentals and only medium on the macro path. The base case at 60 percent, with 75 percent confidence attached, is a soft landing: global GDP 1.5 to 2.5 percent, organic revenue growth 8-10 percent, operating margin steady near 26.5 percent, Chinese luxury spending grinding back to 90 percent of pre-pandemic by mid-2024 rather than snapping back, US high-net-worth demand offsetting a weakening aspirational buyer, and Tiffany synergies continuing. At 24x forward, its five-year average, on 7.50 of EPS, that's 180, about 16 percent up. Bull at 25 percent with only 60 percent confidence, since it hinges on Beijing's policy choices, needs GDP above 3 percent and revenge spending driving organic growth of 14-16 percent with margins to 28 percent, giving 231 at 28x on 8.25. Bear at 15 percent takes it to 130. Weighted that is 184.65, so accumulate: buy at 155, add near 145 support, trim into 180, and exit on a decisive weekly close below 135. The bias I need to confront is status quo anchoring on LVMH's history of resilience, and the alternative reading deserves real weight, that the deceleration from over 20 percent to high single digits is the beginning of a trend rather than normalization, with the aspirational buyer already gone and the top end next, which would make the bear case 30-40 percent likely and the stock a value trap. My falsification tests are two quarters of Fashion and Leather Goods organic growth under 5 percent, margins under 25 percent for two quarters, and Kering or Richemont flagging a sharp Asian demand drop.

This Palantir framing puts the tension exactly where it belongs, a high-growth commercial engine bolted to lumpy politically sensitive government revenue, and my confidence should reflect that split honestly: 80 percent on technicals since the range-bound state is obvious, 65 percent on commercial fundamentals, and only 40 percent on government because contract timing is genuinely opaque. With the stock between a 50-day near 16 and resistance at 20, RSI neutral at 52 and the MACD histogram pinned near zero, the base case at 60 percent is continued consolidation: commercial revenue up 32 percent, government only 12 percent, total around 22 percent, GAAP profitability still out of reach because of stock-based compensation, adjusted operating margin near 20 percent and forward price-to-sales around 18x. I'd expect oscillation between 15.50 and 19.50, so the target is the midpoint at 18.50. Bull at 25 percent needs AIP pulling seven-figure deals at an accelerating clip plus a landmark win like the NHS Federated Data Platform at roughly 480 million pounds, taking it to 25. Bear at 15 percent is commercial decelerating under 25 percent alongside a contract loss and a market-wide multiple compression, 12. The vulnerabilities I have to state plainly: there is no margin of safety at this multiple, so any deceleration gets punished hard; I may be over-crediting management's AIP commentary, which is classic confirmation bias; and my assumption of moderate government contract flow is an educated guess about a black box. In fairness, the SBC that bears call dilution may be necessary talent retention in a fiercely competitive AI market. If the bull case fails, I check net new commercial customer additions, billings growth as the leading metric, and unusual insider selling.

Block over nine months turns on whether Afterpay actually knits the two ecosystems together, and my confidence scores should show the crypto overhang: 65 percent fundamental, 70 percent technical, and only 60 percent on the probability assignments given crypto and competitive uncertainty. Salesforce near 230 with the full technical-plus-fundamental framework, and unlike the more hedged versions of this call I think the numbers here justify an outright buy.
